records.problem: I need to ROT13-encode/decode a string for an obfuscation puzzle.
solutionWeaknesses: cyberchef is heavy for one transform

records.problem: I need to convert text to its binary representation and back for a CS assignment.
I need to escape a block of text so it is a valid JSON string value (quotes, newlines).
I need to compare two CSV files and see which rows were added, removed, or changed.
solutionWeaknesses: uploads sensitive data to a server
userFailures: A semicolon-delimited European export parses as a single column and every row reads as changed.
Two files that differ only in row order are reported as wholly different.

records.problem: My CSV has empty rows, trailing commas and stray whitespace I need cleaned before import.
userFailures: A semicolon-delimited European export parses as one column, silently, so the cleanup applies to nothing.
A trailing empty column from a spreadsheet export survives the clean because it looks like real data.

records.problem: I want to pick out specific columns from a CSV and drop the rest.
userFailures: A semicolon-delimited European export parses as one column, so there are no columns to pick from.
Picking columns by index breaks the moment the source adds a column, when the user meant to pick by header name.

records.problem: I need to convert a comma-separated file to tab-separated for a tool that only accepts TSV.
userFailures: The source uses semicolons rather than commas, so the whole file converts into one column per row.
A field containing a tab breaks the output silently, since TSV has no quoting convention to fall back on.

records.problem: I need a CRC32 checksum of a string to verify a transfer.
userFailures: The user already has a checksum from elsewhere and is comparing eight hex characters by eye.
A trailing newline in the pasted input changes the digest, and nothing says so.

records.problem: I am holding a string that should have decoded cleanly and did not, and I do not know which encoding it actually is.
existingSolutions: trial and error in a REPL
solutionWeaknesses: cyberchef's magic wand is buried and assumes you know to look for it
answers are per-case and not reusable
no tool states WHY a decode failed
userFailures: Pastes standard base64 into a base64url decoder, gets mojibake, and blames the source data.
Decodes once, sees another encoded string, and cannot tell it was double-encoded rather than corrupt.
Assumes a hex digest is base64 because both look like random characters of similar length.
Strips padding that was load-bearing and gets a silently truncated final byte.

latent.whyUnnamed: You cannot search for the encoding of a string while you still believe you know what it is. The query only forms after someone tells you the assumption was wrong, so the search that would find this tool happens after the failure it prevents.
observedBehaviour: Pasting the string into three different decoders in turn until one returns something readable.
Asking a colleague to look at it because it looks like base64 but does not decode.
Shipping the mojibake downstream and discovering it in a customer-facing field.

records.query: which hash algorithm produced this digest
records.problem: I have a digest and a file and I cannot tell whether they disagree because the file is wrong or because I am comparing two different algorithms.
searchQueries: why does my checksum not match
solutionWeaknesses: identifier sites are ad-heavy and upload-based
the CLI requires knowing the algorithm first
userFailures: Compares a SHA-1 against a SHA-256 and concludes the download is corrupt.
Sees an uppercase digest beside a lowercase one and reads a mismatch that is not one.
Cannot distinguish a truncated digest from a different algorithm of the same prefix.
Pastes a digest with a trailing filename from a .sha256 file and gets no match.

latent.whyUnnamed: A digest carries no label. The person holding one believes it is the checksum, singular, so the possibility that they are comparing two different algorithms never becomes a thought, let alone a query.
observedBehaviour: Re-downloading a large file repeatedly because the checksum keeps failing.
Counting digest characters by hand to guess the algorithm.
Abandoning verification entirely and installing the artifact unchecked.

records.problem: A system rejected my UUID and I cannot see what is wrong with it by looking at it.
solutionWeaknesses: a regex confirms shape and says nothing about version or variant
library checks require writing code to answer one question
userFailures: Supplies a v4 UUID where the schema requires v7 and learns it only from a rejected insert.
Pastes a UUID missing one character and the resulting error names an unrelated field.
Treats a v1 UUID as random when it embeds a timestamp and a MAC address.
Generates a nil UUID as a placeholder and it passes shape validation everywhere downstream.

latent.whyUnnamed: A UUID looks correct to a human at every level except the two bits that encode its version and variant. Nobody searches for a checker because nobody can see the thing that is wrong, and the rejection downstream almost never says wrong UUID version.
observedBehaviour: Regenerating the identifier and retrying, hoping the next one is accepted.
Diffing a working UUID against a failing one character by character.
Storing a v1 UUID in a public URL without knowing it leaks a host and a timestamp.

records.query: regex tester with live capture groups
records.problem: I need to test a regular expression against sample text and see every capture group, named group, and match highlight update as I type, without sending my data to a server.
solutionWeaknesses: uploads pattern and sample text to a remote service
editor find shows only the next match, not all groups
userFailures: A greedy quantifier silently swallows the intended capture and the tool only shows the full match, so the group looks empty for the wrong reason.
A multiline sample looks correct until they paste a Windows CRLF string and ^/$ stop matching the lines they expected.
A named group works in one flavor and is treated as a literal in another, and nothing says which flavor is active.
They debug a lookbehind that the browser engine does not support and get a cryptic SyntaxError instead of a flavor note.

records.query: merge split rotate pdf in browser
records.problem: I need to merge, split, rotate, or reorder PDF pages on my machine without uploading confidential documents to a random converter site.
solutionWeaknesses: documents leave the machine and sit on a third-party server
desktop suites are heavy for a one-off reorder
userFailures: Pages land out of order because drag-reorder applied to thumbnails of a different file than the one being exported.
A scanned PDF rotates visually in the preview but the printed page stays landscape because only the view matrix changed.
Merging two PDFs with different page sizes produces a file that print dialogs crop without warning.
A password-protected PDF fails silently mid-merge and the output keeps only the unprotected half.

records.query: convert compress resize image heic online
records.problem: I need to convert, compress, or resize images including HEIC from a phone, entirely in the browser so the photos never upload.
solutionWeaknesses: HEIC support is missing or paywalled
batch limits and watermarks on free tiers
userFailures: A HEIC converts to JPEG but the orientation tag is dropped, so phone photos appear sideways.
Quality slider looks fine in preview and still blows the email attachment size limit because dimensions were never capped.
Transparent PNG becomes a black or white rectangle after JPEG conversion with no alpha warning.
A batch run silently skips one corrupted file and the zip looks complete until someone opens it.

records.problem: I need a structural diff of two JSON documents that understands objects and arrays, not a line-oriented text compare that breaks when keys are reordered.
solutionWeaknesses: text diffs treat key order as a change
array moves show as delete-plus-add with no path
userFailures: Two objects that differ only in key order are reported as wholly different because the tool stringified without sorting keys.
An array of objects with a stable id field is diffed by index, so a reorder looks like every field changed.
A numeric 1 and a string "1" are shown as equal when deep-compare is too loose, or unequal with no type callout when it is strict.
A null vs missing key is collapsed into one red row and the fix goes to the wrong place.

records.query: hash a file in the browser sha256
records.problem: I need the SHA-256 or MD5 of a local file to verify a download, without pasting the whole file into a text hash box or uploading it.
solutionWeaknesses: upload-based hash sites receive the whole artifact
CLI is fine for developers and opaque for everyone else
text hash tools reject binary files or truncate large pastes
userFailures: Compares a file hash against a digest that still has the filename suffix from a .sha256 sidecar and reads a false mismatch.
Hashes a partially downloaded file and concludes the mirror is corrupt.
Picks MD5 because the site defaulted to it while the publisher published SHA-256.
Drops a multi-gigabyte ISO onto a tool that loads the whole file into memory and the tab dies with no progress.
